summary: Describes using DTLS over SCTP, giving privacy for SCTP applications and letting client-server applications communicate in a way designed to prevent eavesdropping and detect tampering.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6083 specifies how to use Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) with Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP). The arrangement protects application data while keeping SCTP's message boundaries and stream choices.

questions: why not use tls over sctp
how does dtls use sctp streams
how are sctp auth keys derived from dtls
subtitle: Run DTLS over SCTP while preserving SCTP messages, streams, and delivery choices.

tldr.problem: TLS over SCTP does not preserve unordered delivery or partial reliability and needs separate TLS connections for bidirectional streams.
tldr.mechanism: DTLS runs within an SCTP association. Each SCTP user message carries one DTLS record, while SCTP handles reliability and fragmentation.
tldr.outcome: Applications can use most SCTP transport features with DTLS privacy and tamper detection. RFC 6083 is updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 6083 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2011. The unit metadata says RFC 8996 updates it.

sections.title: Why Use DTLS with SCTP
sections.content:
Transport Layer Security (TLS) is designed for a reliable, ordered byte stream. Applying TLS to SCTP has limitations: unordered delivery and partial reliability are unavailable, both directions need the same number of streams, and each bidirectional stream needs its own TLS connection.

This RFC specifies DTLS over SCTP instead. It preserves message boundaries and allows applications to use ordered or unordered messages, multiple streams, partial reliability, and SCTP dynamic address reconfiguration.
sections.plainLanguage: DTLS can protect messages carried by SCTP without turning them into one ordered byte stream. This lets an application keep using SCTP's separate streams and delivery options.

sections.title: DTLS Features Handled by SCTP
sections.content:
SCTP already provides reliable delivery when requested, fragmentation and reassembly, and Path MTU discovery. The DTLS layer therefore MUST NOT use its own retransmission, replay detection, or Path MTU discovery procedures for this arrangement.

For DTLS over SCTP, the DTLS path MTU is considered to be 2^14. This is also the maximum user message size stated for the method. SCTP implementation support for user-message fragmentation is required.
sections.plainLanguage: SCTP already handles delivery and packet sizing for these messages. DTLS turns off overlapping functions so the two layers do not compete.

sections.title: Mapping SCTP Messages to DTLS Records
sections.content:
Every SCTP user message MUST contain exactly one DTLS record. The supported maximum SCTP user-message length MUST be at least 18445 bytes, which the RFC derives from the largest DTLS ciphertext fragment and the DTLS record header.

A DTLS connection MUST be established and terminated within one SCTP association; it cannot span multiple associations. Application protocols SHOULD use a separate Payload Protocol Identifier for DTLS-protected traffic rather than reuse the identifier for plain SCTP traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: Each SCTP message carries one complete DTLS record. A DTLS connection belongs to one SCTP association and cannot continue across another association.

sections.title: Streams and Delivery Order
sections.content:
ChangeCipherSpec, Alert, and Handshake messages MUST use stream 0 with ordered delivery and unlimited reliability. ApplicationData SHOULD use other streams, but may use stream 0 when head-of-line blocking is not a concern.

SCTP DATA chunks MUST be authenticated so an attacker cannot change the stream identifier or ordered/unordered flag. If partial-reliability SCTP is used, FORWARD-TSN chunks MUST also be authenticated.
sections.plainLanguage: DTLS setup and control messages use stream zero and arrive in order. Application data can use other streams, and SCTP chunk authentication protects the stream and delivery settings.

sections.title: Handshake Changes and Shared Keys
sections.content:
Before sending ChangeCipherSpec, the sender MUST wait until all outstanding SCTP user messages are acknowledged and cannot be revoked. Before processing a received ChangeCipherSpec, buffered SCTP messages must be read and processed. New-epoch messages arriving between ChangeCipherSpec and Finished are buffered until Finished is read.

When the DTLS master key changes, a 64-byte shared secret is derived using the exporter label EXPORTER_DTLS_OVER_SCTP. The Shared Key Identifier increments by one, except that after 65535 it becomes 1. The active SCTP-AUTH key changes before Finished is sent.
sections.plainLanguage: Key changes wait until earlier SCTP messages are safely delivered. DTLS derives a shared secret for SCTP authentication whenever its master key changes.

sections.title: What DTLS Does Not Hide
sections.content:
The security considerations of the cited DTLS and SCTP specifications also apply. Security decisions should rely on the authenticated identity of the peer, not on the IP address from which a record arrives, because an SCTP endpoint can use several addresses.

DTLS protects the application message but not the SCTP stream identifier, ordered/unordered flag, or Payload Protocol Identifier; those values are sent in the SCTP DATA chunk header. A negotiated NULL cipher provides no privacy.
sections.plainLanguage: DTLS protects the record contents, but some SCTP delivery information remains visible. A NULL cipher also means the message has no privacy protection.
